opeds.headline: Meta's Future Has Owners. Name Them.
opeds.subtitle: The 'everyone' campaign is an infrastructure pitch with the water bill left off the page.
opeds.body:
In Altoona, Iowa, the water that cools Meta's servers does not come from a slogan. It comes from a municipal system that already has to decide whose lawns go brown in a dry July. The company calls the campus a piece of the future. The utility calls it load.

This month, as Senate committees take up another round of artificial-intelligence bills and Meta's people work the hallways, the company is pushing a campaign titled "The Future Is for Everyone." The site is clean. The promise is that the next wave of software will lift people rather than replace them, connect rather than extract, and belong to the public rather than to a handful of firms.

Treat that campaign as an infrastructure and extraction project, not a vision statement. Name who owns the compute, who sells the link between your records, who labels the material that trains the model, and which human being signs the release. Then write the rules for those people. Not for "AI." For them.

The everyone story is doing a job. It is not describing a machine. It is recruiting a permission structure — from Congress, from city councils, from the people whose attention and photographs become training stock — so the buildout can proceed with the politics already settled. Grand rescue and grand ruin are both useful here. Both make the firm look like a historical force instead of a landlord of chips, fiber, and contracts.

Here is what that looks like on the ground. A data hall is a warehouse of processors, a substation, a water permit, and a tax abatement. The chips still travel a supply chain that runs through a few foundries and a few countries. The power still hits a grid that was not built for this density. None of that is unprecedented. It is the same physical arithmetic that governed railroad spurs and telecom hotels, dressed now as destiny.

Translate that into a person. There is a contractor in Nairobi opening a queue of the worst things human beings post, so a model can be declared safe enough to ship. The wage is a few dollars an hour. The injury is not theoretical. Meta does not put that worker on the campaign site. The site needs the labor to disappear so the product can look like weather — something that just arrives, for everyone.

Now ask who pays. The financial windfall concentrates where the compute, the ad auction, and the distribution already sit. The operational mess — traumatized moderators, drained aquifers, towns bidding against each other with tax breaks, users who never consented to have their lives melted into weights — lands somewhere else. That is not a side effect of a democratizing technology. That is the business.

The campaign also skips the market that prices you before any chatbot ever answers. Data brokers already buy, match, and resell the links between your records. The identity graph is assembled upstream of the cute interface. Rules bolted onto the deployed assistant govern the last mile and leave the chokepoint untouched. If you only regulate the talking box, you have regulated the storefront and ignored the warehouse.

Privacy is not a settings panel. It is a boundary on extraction. Training a commercial model on people who did not agree to be ore is not openness. It is a taking. A future that is actually for everyone would start by making that taking expensive, visible, and in many cases illegal — not by inviting the public to feel included in a product built from them.

To be sure, Meta has released model weights that competitors have kept locked. That is real, and the closed labs hate it for reasons that are not all noble. Open weights are not the same thing as an open system. The data diet stays proprietary. The cheapest, largest training runs still require a capital stack most universities and most countries cannot touch. The attention market that funds the whole apparatus stays Meta's. Handing out a file while owning the mine, the smelter, and the store is not a commons. It is a distribution tactic.

Insurance floors, capital requirements, and a named department on a masthead will tell you who writes a check after someone is hurt. They will not tell you what duty a human being owed before the ship button was hit. Solvency is not care. A payout is not a standard. If the only question the statute can answer is who pays the claim, the statute has already accepted the harm as a cost of goods.

Congress should stop writing hymns to innovation and start writing names. Amend Section 230 with a scalpel, not a wrecking ball: keep the core shield for ordinary user speech, and restore liability where a company builds, trains, and deploys a system that causes the harm — especially where it has ingested people as raw material. Require a named officer, not a safety team, to sign an enumerated hazard checklist on each release and keep that signature as the liability record. If the release later maims someone, the record is a person, not a department.

The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general should treat the broker layer as the actual market, not a footnote. Ban the non-consensual sale of linkage that makes re-identification a product. Force disclosure of what went into the training mix in language a juror can read. Meta's board should be asked, in public, for the water, power, and labor ledgers of every campus it wants subsidized — not the carbon brochure, the invoices.

City councils holding the next abatement vote can do one useful thing: put the utility's numbers on the same page as the jobs slide. If the future is for everyone, the drawdown should be too.

The people selling salvation and the people selling extinction are useful to each other. Both need the public staring at a horizon so nobody inventories the building. The building has a meter. The meter has a name on the account.

When the next hearing opens with a slide about opportunity, ask the witness who signed the last release, who got paid to look at the worst of it, and what the Iowa utility will do in July. Then ask why "everyone" is not in the room.
opeds.pitch:
Subject: Op-Ed Submission: Meta's Future Has Owners. Name Them.

This month, as Senate committees take up AI bills and Meta pushes its "The Future Is for Everyone" campaign, this essay argues the slogan is an infrastructure-and-extraction pitch, not a public vision — and that Congress should pin release liability on named officers, cut a surgical Section 230 fix, and police the data-broker layer upstream of the chatbot. The piece offers a material ledger (power, water, contracted labor, consent) against the everyone narrative.

[Author] is a technology and political-economy writer focused on infrastructure, labor, and corporate accountability.

The full draft is pasted below.

grounding.label: Downstream Gates Miss the Broker-Aggregation Layer Where Linkage Is Priced
grounding.how_reflected: It is reflected after the third evidence pillar in the data-broker paragraph and again in the FTC portion of the solution/call-to-action, contributing the claim that rules bolted onto the deployed assistant govern the last mile and leave the upstream broker-aggregation layer where linkage is priced untouched.

grounding.label: Solvency Mechanisms Locate a Payer Without Preserving a Duty of Care
grounding.how_reflected: It is reflected in the paragraph immediately before the solution/call-to-action, contributing the argument that insurance floors, capital requirements, and a named department locate a payer after harm without preserving a prior duty of care.

grounding.label: Privacy as a Non-Negotiable Right in AI
grounding.how_reflected: It is reflected in the privacy paragraph after the broker discussion, contributing the insistence that privacy is a non-negotiable boundary on extraction (a taking that should be expensive, visible, and often illegal) rather than a settings panel.

grounding.label: Surgical Realignment of Liability
grounding.how_reflected: It is reflected in the solution/call-to-action, contributing the surgical Section 230 amendment (scalpel, not wrecking ball) that keeps the core shield for ordinary user speech while restoring liability where a company builds, trains, and deploys a harmful system.

grounding.label: Pin AI Safety Liability to Named Individuals, Not Departments, for Each Release
grounding.how_reflected: It is reflected in the solution/call-to-action and echoed in the closing, contributing the requirement that a named officer—not a safety team or department—sign an enumerated hazard checklist on each release as the liability record.

grounding.label: Sociotechnical Complexity in AI Systems
grounding.how_reflected: It is reflected in the thesis and first evidence pillar, contributing the framing of the campus as a sociotechnical stack (warehouse of processors, substation, water permit, tax abatement, foundries, grid, labor, and contracts) rather than a slogan or disembodied vision.
